questions.model_answer: I usually decide as I cook, because a strict recipe feels slow on a weeknight. I repeat a few combinations I already know, and that keeps dinner simple.

questions.set_intro: Imagine that a marketing firm is researching daily habits in your area. You agreed to take part in a telephone interview about cooking at home.
questions.question: A friend wants to cook more meals at home but feels too busy. What would you recommend, and why?
questions.model_answer: I would tell my friend to start with three simple meals and repeat them. A short list removes decisions, and each dish gets faster every time you cook it. I would also suggest cutting vegetables on Sunday, so a weeknight only needs a pan and twenty minutes. That plan is easier to keep than a new complicated dish every evening.

questions.question: Some companies let employees choose their start and finish times. Do you think flexible work hours are a good idea? Give reasons for your opinion.
questions.model_answer: I think flexible work hours are a good idea for most office teams. People do their best thinking at different times of day, so a choice of start time can raise the quality of the work. For example, an early riser might begin at seven and finish in the middle of the afternoon, while a colleague with a long bus ride might start after the rush and stay later. That kind of choice also helps parents and students handle duties outside the job without missing a deadline. The limit is that a team still needs shared time. If everyone is available from ten to three for meetings and quick questions, and if the manager judges results rather than the clock, flexibility helps both the workers and the company.
